full_text:

The rout followed Wall Street's steepest single-day decline in more than a year on Thursday. The S&P 500 tumbled 4.4%, the Nasdaq Composite slumped 5.5% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 3.4%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.3%.
U.S. stock futures traded higher in Asian trading Friday by 02:33 GMT.

KOSPI last traded 4.1% lower, with Samsung Electronics (KS:005930) falling 4.1%, and SK Hynix (KS:000660) sliding 7%.

The election outcome has added another layer of uncertainty. Democrats' gains in the midterms have raised concerns that a Democrat-controlled Congress could increase scrutiny of data-centre developments and potentially slow construction, particularly in states where candidates campaigned against large-scale projects.

China's Shanghai Composite fell 1%, while the clue-chip Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped 1.3%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index edged 0.3% lower.
Singapore's Straits Times Index dropped 2.4%, while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 1%.
Futures tied to India's Nifty 50 inched down 0.3%.
While expectations that Democrats' election victory could accelerate efforts to end the Iran war had initially supported risk appetite, concerns over AI investment and semiconductor earnings have since taken centre stage.

title: Trump blames Democrats for Wall Street selloff after historic midterm election win
full_text:
Investing.com -- U.S. President Donald Trump blamed Democrats for Wall Street's sharp selloff following their sweeping midterm election victories, saying the stock market had suffered one of its worst days in history and warning that Americans' 401(k) retirement accounts had taken a hit.
Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday's November 3 elections, flipping at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts in a major setback for Republicans.
The results also included Democratic victories in key gubernatorial races and widespread support for local measures restricting data-centre developments.
Wall Street initially welcomed the outcome. On Wednesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.4%, as investors anticipated reduced political uncertainty.
However, that rally reversed sharply on Thursday as investors reassessed the implications of Democratic victories for the artificial intelligence industry.
The S&P 500 dropped 4.4% to 7,353.73, its steepest decline since the April 2025 tariff selloff. The Dow lost 1,833 points, or 3.4%, while the Nasdaq plunged 5.5%, its worst session in 18 months. The Russell 2000 also fell 4.4%.
The losses were concentrated in technology and semiconductor stocks amid concerns that Democratic lawmakers and newly elected governors could introduce tighter restrictions on data-centre construction, potentially slowing the expansion of AI infrastructure.
At least 38 jurisdictions passed restrictions or bans on data-centre projects, while Texas' incoming Democratic Governor Gina Hinojosa has advocated a moratorium on new developments.
Nvidia fell around 9%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 17% and Micron declined more than 17%.
The Nasdaq's market capitalisation shed about $2 trillion during Thursday's selloff, according to Reuters, as investors reassessed the growth outlook for AI infrastructure.
While the Dow's decline marked its worst second trading session following a midterm election in records dating back to 1896, Thursday's broader market losses were not unprecedented. The S&P 500's 4.4% decline was its largest since April 2025.

full_text:

Investors also weighed renewed equity-market losses against expectations of a shift in U.S. fiscal and monetary policy.

title: Lotte Rental shares hit 52-week high as TPG launches $613 million tender offer
full_text:
Investing.com -- Lotte Rental (KS:089860) shares surged over 10% on Friday after TPG-backed Lexicon Korea Holdco launched an 831.7 billion won ($613 million) tender offer for the remaining stake in the South Korean car rental company, seeking to take it private and pursue a voluntary delisting.
The shares rose 10.4% to a 52-week high of 58,400 won in early trade, while the benchmark KOSPI plunged as much as 8.5% before a 20-minute circuit breaker was triggered at 9:03 a.m. Seoul time.

Lexicon, a special-purpose vehicle backed by TPG, already owns 61.17% of Lotte Rental after acquiring 22.2 million shares from Hotel Lotte and Busan Lotte Hotel for 1.31 trillion won on October 30. The latest offer would bring its ownership to 100% if all remaining shares are acquired, taking TPG's total investment to about 2.14 trillion won.
The tender offer prospectus states that Lexicon intends to make Lotte Rental a wholly owned subsidiary and pursue its voluntary delisting, subject to the offer outcome and applicable regulatory requirements. The bidder has set no minimum acceptance threshold and intends to purchase all shares validly tendered.
Lotte Rental operates long- and short-term vehicle rental services, used-car sales and business equipment rental operations.

title: Exclusive-China’s top flash memory chipmaker targets more homegrown tools for new factory, sources say
full_text:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - China’s largest flash memory chipmaker, Yangtze Memory Technologies Co (YMTC), plans to source as much as 70% of the equipment for a planned fourth factory from domestic suppliers, two people familiar with the matter said.
The target would be a step up from the share at YMTC’s third factory, which is due to begin operating later this year, where Chinese suppliers account for just over half of equipment purchases. The plan offers a fresh measure of China’s progress in replacing foreign chipmaking tools.
The planned fourth factory in Wuhan, where YMTC is based, is expected to make the company’s most advanced NAND chips, with more than 300 layers of memory cells stacked vertically, the people said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
The plant is expected to focus mainly on storage chips for data centres and artificial intelligence applications.
NAND flash memory retains data when devices are switched off and is used in smartphones, computers and data centres. Stacking more layers of memory cells vertically increases storage density, meaning it allows more data to be stored on a chip of the same physical size.
YMTC is targeting a domestic-equipment share of at least 60% at the new plant, with an ambition to reach 70%, the people said. Construction is expected to begin next year, though YMTC has so far only held preliminary discussions with suppliers and has not placed formal orders.
The timing of the fourth factory and its domestic-equipment target are being reported for the first time.
The plans come as US export controls constrain YMTC’s access to some American chipmaking technology. They also complicate efforts by South Korean rivals like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix to expand capacity or make major technology upgrades at their factories in China.
YMTC’s new plant would give it a higher memory cell layer count than its rivals are able to produce in China. Samsung is converting its Xian factory to make 286-layer chips, while SK Hynix is upgrading a Dalian facility to 240 layers or more from 192, Reuters previously reported.
YMTC’s NAND market share in China rose to 38.5% in the second quarter from 28% in 2025, with the company overtaking Samsung as the top NAND maker in the country, according to data from Omdia, a market research firm.
YMTC, Samsung, and the US Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment. SK Hynix declined to comment.
BOON FOR CHINESE EQUIPMENT MAKERS
The higher local-content target could benefit Chinese equipment makers including Naura Technology Group and Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment, the sources said.
Most of the additional domestic orders are expected to come from workhorse stages of production, including cleaning, polishing and etching wafers, where Chinese suppliers have already proven their equipment on YMTC’s production lines, the people said.
Chinese firms already supply most of YMTC’s cleaning and polishing tools and have made progress in equipment used to form the deep vertical structures required for advanced NAND chips.
YMTC nonetheless remains reliant on overseas suppliers for some sophisticated tools, including in lithography, inspection, and other advanced manufacturing processes.
US RESTRICTIONS DRIVE LOCALISATION
The US Commerce Department added YMTC to its Entity List in December 2022, imposing licensing requirements on US suppliers that were seeking to sell certain technology to the company.
Samsung and SK Hynix require annual US authorisations to bring American-made chipmaking equipment into their Chinese plants. Washington indicated last year that it did not intend to approve equipment that would allow the companies to substantially increase capacity or make major technology upgrades there.
In April, Reuters reported that YMTC was planning to build two additional factories in Wuhan, giving the chipmaker a total of five.
When fully operational, the third, fourth, and fifth factories are each expected to process about 100,000 silicon wafers a month, the sources said. Together, they would more than double YMTC’s manufacturing capacity.

title: HKEX shares fall nearly 2% as Q3 profit slips amid slower market activity
full_text:
Investing.com -- Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HK:0388) shares fell on Friday after the exchange operator reported a decline in third-quarter profit due to softer activity in its cash and Southbound Stock Connect markets.
The shares were down 1.7% at HK$387.80, underperforming the Hang Seng Index, which tarded 0.5% lower.

Core business revenue was flat at HK$7.47 billion, despite an 11% decline in headline average daily turnover on the Stock Exchange to HK$254.2 billion.
Lower Cash Market and Southbound Stock Connect trading and clearing fees, as well as reduced net investment income from margin funds due to higher rebates to clearing participants, offset gains from commodities trading, Northbound Stock Connect activity and higher listing fees.
Operating expenses rose 8% to HK$1.60 billion, mainly due to higher staff and information technology costs.
Despite the softer quarter, HKEX reported record revenue and profit for the first nine months of 2026.
Revenue and other income rose 12% year on year to HK$24.57 billion, while profit attributable to shareholders increased 15% to HK$15.43 billion. EBITDA climbed 14% to HK$19.61 billion, with its margin widening one percentage point to 80%.
Hong Kong also ranked as the world's second-largest IPO market by funds raised during the period. A total of 118 new listings raised HK$388.4 billion, more than double the year-earlier amount, while follow-on fundraising reached a record HK$572.8 billion, up 25%.

title: Asian FX mixed as yen gains on risk aversion, Taiwan dollar breaks 33 amid AI rout
full_text:
Investing.com -- Asian currencies traded mixed on Friday as a sharp selloff in U.S. technology shares drove investors towards haven assets, supporting the Japanese yen, while the Taiwan dollar briefly weakened past a key psychological level.
The U.S. dollar held broadly steady ahead of October payrolls as markets reassessed the Federal Reserve's interest-rate outlook.
The U.S. dollar index rose 0.1% to 101.70. The USD/JPY pair was up 0.1% at 157.85 after the yen earlier strengthened to a one-week high near 157.40.
The USD/TWD pair stood at 32.988, down 0.3%, after briefly rising above 33. The USD/KRW pair gained 0.2% to 1,360.36, while USD/CNH and USD/CNY were little changed. The Australian and New Zealand dollars fell 0.3% to $0.6914 and $0.5580, while the Singapore dollar weakened 0.2%.
Yen draws safe-haven demand as AI selloff rattles markets
The yen strengthened as much as 0.6% to 157.54 per dollar, outperforming all Group-of-10 currencies as a sharp Wall Street selloff triggered a shift towards safer assets.
The Nasdaq plunged 5.52%, its steepest one-day drop since April 2025, while the S&P 500 fell 4.36%. Investors feared that Democrats' sweeping midterm victory could lead to tighter scrutiny of artificial-intelligence investment, particularly data-centre construction, prompting a retreat from equities into bonds and haven currencies. The yen subsequently surrendered some of its gains.
The move has revived its traditional safe-haven appeal. During a similar technology-stock selloff last month, the currency briefly strengthened to 156.08 per dollar before reversing much of that advance.
Elsewhere, the Taiwan dollar fell as much as 0.5% to 33.040 per dollar, its weakest since April 2025 and its first break above 33 since then. It was Asia's worst performer as Taiwan shares dropped around 6% amid foreign outflows, although it later recovered below 33.
The won also faced equity-driven pressure. The KOSPI plunged 8.6%, falling below 5,000 for the first time in nine months and triggering a 20-minute trading halt. Foreign investors sold 3.39 trillion won of shares on Thursday. The dollar-won rate had risen 1.16% from the previous weekly close to around 1,357.9 before reaching 1,360.36.
Kiwi and yuan face pressure as regional data shape currency outlook
The New Zealand dollar has fallen around 11% since the pandemic, making it the second-worst-performing G10 currency after the yen. Sluggish growth and a weak labour market have weighed on the kiwi, which recently hit a record low against the offshore yuan and its weakest level against the Australian dollar in nearly 14 years, raising import costs ahead of the election.
The yuan has retreated after reaching a more than four-year high near 6.659 per dollar last week. It had been heading for a fifth consecutive weekly gain and fourth monthly advance, supported by exporter conversions, before the PBOC raised banks' foreign-exchange reserve requirement from 4% to 6% from November 15.

title: Goldman lowers year-end gold price forecast on hawkish Fed shift
full_text:
Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs slashed its gold price forecasts, citing the Federal Reserve’s hawkish shift in recent months and its effect on investor positioning, while keeping a constructive longer-term view tied to strong central bank buying.
Strategists led by Lina Thomas lowered their end-2026 forecast to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650, and their end-2027 forecast to $4,800 from $5,400. Goldman’s base case assumes the Fed’s recent hawkish shift and a December rate hike will keep investor "debasement concerns" contained.
As a result, the bank expects demand for gold as a hedge against macro-policy risks, reflected in call-option demand, to normalize toward its historical average instead of returning to elevated levels seen earlier this year.
The setup increasingly resembles 2022, when central banks provided a strong structural bid but higher interest rates weighed on investor positioning, producing a more modest pace of price gains, the strategists said.
Central bank demand remains the primary support, with Goldman expecting purchases of 60 tonnes a month through 2026 and 2027, versus a pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes. Its nowcast puts current purchases at 85 tonnes a month on a seasonally adjusted three-month basis.
"We retain our longer-term constructive view on structurally strong central bank demand – which drives most of the 15% price upside we forecast by end-2027," the strategists wrote.
They said emerging-market central banks, particularly China, remain underweight gold relative to plausible long-term allocations. Developed-market central banks have largely stayed out of the buying wave, in part because they already hold significant gold reserves for historical reasons.
"But the debate is increasingly shifting from whether to own gold to where to store it, pointing to broader concerns around reserve security and cross-country trust," the strategists continued.
Goldman expects further price support once the Fed starts cutting rates in the second half of 2027. The bank’s economists forecast cuts from late 2027 through early 2028, which should lift the rate constraint on gold and let private investor demand compete again with central bank buying.
The outlook varies by horizon, strategists noted. For CTAs and macro hedge funds, the next three to six months remain challenging given a rising funds rate, uncertain energy prices and tight drawdown limits. Higher oil prices could add pressure through systematic selling.
Longer-horizon investors seeking exposure to central bank demand or protection against policy tail risks may find the current correction an attractive entry point, they said.
Goldman sees further downside risk if the Fed hikes again in March 2027, delays cuts or raises its terminal rate. In that scenario, it estimates gold would reach $4,660 by the end of 2027. Fiscal sustainability concerns could revive hedge demand and provide upside beyond its base case of 4,800 by the end of 2027, the strategists said.

title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production at Texas factory as it struggles to win appeal
full_text:
By Ananya Palyekar
Nov 6 (Reuters) - Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, as the model once touted as a futuristic rival to legacy pickup trucks struggles to win mass-market appeal.
While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility, or phased out entirely, the automaker’s Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model’s specialized components.
Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours.
In an X post, Musk said the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased production of its newly launched Cybercab model, which Musk has made central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions.
Musk has said he sees it as Tesla’s main autonomous model within a larger driverless network as he aims to transform the electric vehicle maker into a robotics and self-driving company.
"Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.
"POLARIZING" TECH
Musk had, during Cybertruck’s launch in 2023, touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford. But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations.
Often described as polarizing, Cybertruck’s unorthodox sharp-edged stainless-steel design has limited its prospects outside the US. Regulatory approval became difficult to come by in parts of Europe, depriving Tesla of major markets that could have helped turn the pickup into a higher-volume product.
The model has also faced multiple recalls and quality-control issues, while Tesla has repeatedly revised prices.
Tesla does not officially disclose individual sales figures for the Cybertruck. Instead, the automaker groups it into an "Other Models" category, which accounted for just 8,295 deliveries in the third quarter, down from 12,364 deliveries in the second quarter.

Order backlog was €4.31 billion at the end of September, up 3% from the end of 2025 but below €4.33 billion at the end of June.

Krones described customer demand as "robust overall", but said rising operating costs for customers because of the geopolitical situation are having "some impact" on orders, which it has largely offset with its mix of customers and products.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose 5.2% to €453.1 million from €430.7 million.
The EBITDA margin was 11.1% versus 10.5% a year earlier, including a gain of about €10 million from U.S. tariff refunds; without it, the margin was 10.8%. Krones credited measures to improve performance and cost structures and said prices for its machines and lines were stable overall. Net income rose 2.7% to €219.5 million, or €6.94 per share versus €6.75.

title: Cellnex says Poland deal cuts 2027 cash flow by €300 mln, Q3 in line
full_text:
Investing.com -- Cellnex shares were little changed on Friday after the Spanish telecoms tower operator said a €500 million investment in Poland would reduce its 2027 free cash flow by about €300 million, although it reiterated its guidance and reported third-quarter results broadly in line with expectations.
The project, agreed with client Polkomtel, involves about €500 million in additional capital expenditure between 2026 and 2030, around 3,200 new co-locations by 2030 and a further 2,000 committed beyond that date, as well as about 4,200 antenna relocations and site decommissionings.
Cellnex expects a double-digit unlevered post-tax return, twice its cost of capital.
Cellnex reiterated its 2026 guidance, including free cash flow of €600 million to €700 million, and its 2027 like-for-like free cash flow target of €975 million to €1.18 billion.
The only update was the estimated €300 million impact of the Polish investment and the faster delivery of build-to-suit work already planned.
Jefferies, which rates the shares "buy" and raised its price target to €35 from €34, estimated the investment would reduce 2027 free cash flow to about €675 million to €875 million, all else equal.
Third-quarter revenue excluding pass-through was €1.01 billion, against consensus of €1.02 billion, and increased by €18 million year on year, Jefferies data showed.
Adjusted EBITDA rose by €32 million from a year earlier to €863 million, slightly above the €860 million consensus. EBITDAaL was €658 million, compared with expectations of €655 million.
Recurring levered free cash flow was €471 million, 0.4% below the €473 million consensus, while free cash flow was €172 million, above expectations of €162 million, helped by lower build-to-suit capital expenditure.
Adjusted EBITDA missed expectations in Italy, at €165 million versus €175 million, and France, at €215 million versus €225 million. It beat consensus in the UK, at €136 million versus €125 million, and Poland, at €121 million versus €114 million.
For the first nine months, free cash flow more than doubled to €474 million from €186 million a year earlier, supported by a 22% decline in growth investment to €860 million from €1.11 billion.
Like-for-like operating expenses fell 4.4%, despite Cellnex operating about 2,900 more towers, while its adjusted EBITDA margin increased to 84.8% from 83.1%.
Net debt stood at €21.04 billion at the end of September, up from €20.82 billion at the end of 2025. However, net debt to adjusted EBITDA improved to 6.13 times from 6.28 times on higher earnings. Cellnex said it remained on track to reach its target of 5-6 times in 2027.
The company also remained on track to return €1 billion to shareholders in 2026, having delivered €924 million by September 30.
Chief Executive Marco Patuano said the additional near-term investment "serves a clear long-term ambition by unlocking greater value from our assets."

title: Glanbia shares tumble 6% after Morgan Stanley cuts rating to underweight
full_text:
Investing.com -- Glanbia shares fell sharply on Friday after Morgan Stanley downgraded the Irish nutrition group to Underweight from Equal-weight, warning that intensifying competition and higher contracted whey costs could put pressure on its 2027 margins and earnings.
The shares dropped 6% to €19.95, sharply underperforming the ISEQ Overall, which was last quoted 0.3% lower. The bank cut its 12-month price target to €19.20 from €21.90, implying 9.5% downside from Thursday's closing price of €21.22.
Glanbia shares have rallied around 45% so far this year, with their valuation multiple expanding about 20%, leaving less room for potential earnings disappointment, Morgan Stanley said.
The bank's concern centres on the timing of lower whey costs. Glanbia typically secures its whey supplies six to nine months in advance and still expects higher procurement costs in the first half of 2027.
Competitors with shorter purchasing commitments could access cheaper supplies sooner and use the savings to increase promotions or improve consumer pricing.
Morgan Stanley cited recent disclosures from THG, the owner of Myprotein, which indicated that its WPC80 whey protein concentrate index had fallen around 20% since September and that it had secured fourth-quarter requirements more cheaply than in the third quarter, with further lower-cost coverage for early 2027.
The bank said this could make it harder for Glanbia to sustain further price increases without sacrificing volumes or market share, particularly after several rounds of consumer price increases.
Morgan Stanley lowered its 2027 earnings-per-share estimate by 4%, leaving it 6% below market consensus. It forecasts Performance Nutrition EBITDA of $265 million, around 10% below consensus, as higher contracted whey costs and increased competitive pricing investment weigh on the division's margin recovery.
Morgan Stanley raised its 2026 EPS estimate by 2% following Glanbia's third-quarter results beat, but said the outlook for the following year had become less favourable.

title: Take Five: Tech wreck and roll
full_text:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - Traders on the world’s financial markets go into next week hoping the storm engulfing tech stocks blows itself out and for no new escalation in the Iran war that sends oil prices surging again.
There are also key US and Chinese data, the UN’s COP climate summit gets underway in Turkey, Europe will be horse trading over the next ECB chief and there’s a too-close-to-call election in New Zealand this weekend.
Here’s all you need to know about the coming week in financial markets by Dhara Ranasinghe, Alun John and Simon Jessop in London, Lewis Krauskopf in New York and Gregor Stuart Hunter in Singapore.
1/ HOUSE OF P-AI-N
The Democrats’ US midterm win is the latest hammer blow to the once-unstoppable Big Tech trade.
The Nasdaq’s 5.5% slump on Thursday was its biggest since the Liberation Day rout of April 2025 and wiped $2.5 trillion off that one index alone.
Worries had already been intensifying about the stratospheric cost of the AI buildout. Now, post-midterms, the prospect of tougher regulations that slow everything down is hurting just as much.
Democratic wins in Texas and Georgia reflected the voter backlash against the data centres that are at the heart of the AI boom, but are also ugly and loud and require huge amounts of energy and water.
Some sense a compromise might be struck since AI has become a key economic driver. But if the rout resumes next week, growth worries will likely mount and plenty will be wondering whether something somewhere in the financial system tied to it all might break.
2/KEEPING A CLOSE CPI
US data and the direction of oil prices over the next week could determine whether the Federal Reserve hikes its interest rates one more time before the year is out.
Tuesday’s US consumer price index (CPI) — perhaps the most closely watched inflation measure — is expected to show a monthly rise of 0.3%, according to a Reuters poll, while Friday brings another key read on producer prices.
As it stands, traders are pricing in a more than 80% chance of a Fed hike at its December 8-9 meeting. That would take the federal funds rate — the primary driver of global borrowing costs — to 4.00%-4.25% and follow the Fed’s first rise in three years back in September.
Then there’s oil. Crude prices have pulled back this week after the Republicans’ hammering in the US midterms stoked bets that President Donald Trump may look to de-escalate the Iran war. Any signal either way on that will be pivotal.
3/WHO’S IT GOING TO EC-BE?
European economic growth has been surprisingly resilient this year in the face of sky-high energy prices and rising borrowing costs.
The coming week will provide another test with quarterly employment data due, as well as a more refined estimate of quarterly GDP. Last month’s preliminary flash Q3 reading showed 0.4% growth.
If confirmed, it would boost the mood at Monday’s gathering of euro zone finance ministers, where another top topic will be who replaces European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde when she leaves Frankfurt in February.
Nominations are about to be finalised and the expected candidates are former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the head of the Bank for International Settlements.
The EU hopes to appoint a new ECB president by its mid-December summit, so it will have to get a move on. Monday’s meeting could be busy.
4/COP SHOW
The UN’s COP31 climate summit kicks off in Turkey on Monday, with more than 80 world leaders expected to attend against the backdrop of worsening extreme weather events that have caused a slew of devastating disasters this year.
With the US not formally involved under climate-sceptic Donald Trump, his humbling in this week’s midterms will be a glimmer of hope for some, although efforts to build coalitions of the willing to phase out fossil fuels and halt deforestation will need to continue.
As the Middle East war keeps oil and gas prices high, host Turkey is also pushing nations to accelerate the shift to green power so that 35% of the world’s power comes from electricity by 2035, from around 23% now.
Overhanging everything, though, will be the thorny issue of money. With development aid getting slashed by many richer countries, vulnerable developing countries will once again be looking for more help to cope with climate change.
5/THRILLER IN MANILA
There will be a flurry of last-minute diplomacy in Manila next week as senior government officials start the final preparations on Friday for the following week’s ASEAN nations summit.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, who is hosting the November 15-17 gathering, has said Chinese Premier Li Qiang will be there, while both President Trump and his Canadian sparring partner, Prime Minister Mark Carney, are expected to attend too.
Indonesia is also likely to come under pressure for its wildfires that blanketed much of the region in thick smog earlier this year, with Singapore already vowing to strengthen an agreement on transboundary haze.
Elsewhere in Asia, China releases inflation data for October on Monday and lending data later in the week, while voters in New Zealand go to the polls on Saturday in an election that looks far too close to call.
